columns.note: The 1997 drawings show existing roof columns on a ~44.5 ft grid, two inside each 11,000 SF main room. Every plan with halls takes them out and adds long steel beams (transfer girders) to hold the roof, so both rooms are open. A structural engineer must confirm the framing, footings and clear height before any binding commitment.

optimistic: The floor is confirmed above 250 ft

USGS lidar puts the ground 2–4 ft above the 248 ft flood level along about 85% of the walls. If an elevation certificate confirms the floor, flood work drops to the survey and fixes at the rear dock area.
Bids come in under desk estimates

Roof, HVAC and parking are the biggest swings. County permits show $249,911 of repairs in 2020 and a $423,850 alteration in 2012, so some systems may be newer than assumed. Coating a sound roof instead of replacing it saves about $0.3–0.6M.

Once the halls have reviews, premium Memphis venues ask $10,000–12,000 for a 300–400 guest Saturday (the Cadre Building $12,200; Memphis Botanic Garden $10,000), and a full room for 650–700 guests rents for $11,000–15,000. The average case assumes about $5,550 per event across all days.
Hall demand beats 215 events a year

Daytime and evening events on weekends, weekday corporate and church business, and lower off-peak prices can push bookings toward 260–300 a year once each room can be split. About 1,100–1,200 girls in the metro’s Hispanic community turn 15 each year, and the largest listed banquet halls in Jackson, MS hold about 350 guests.

No hall outside the hotels seating 500 or more was found in northeast Memphis, Raleigh or Bartlett. The nearest are in Cordova and Germantown (FedEx Event Center, about 500 seated; Esplanade, 400) and downtown (The Kent, 600), and the 900-seat ballroom at the former Memphis Vitality Hotel has closed.
A credit fuel tenant on the frontage and a quick-service pad on Summer Avenue add about $146k a year in the best case, and up to $230k a year if both lease at the top of the market.
SBA 504 loans need the owners’ business to occupy at least 51% of an existing building. The halls alone are about 37%; running the kids’ center as well brings it to about 52%.
pessimistic: Shops lease slowly
The retail sits deep in the site behind other buildings, and Summer Avenue is under construction until mid-2028.
Large as-is blocks sit empty
The building is empty, large blocks lease slowly, and Memphis big-box vacancy rose in 2026 as furniture stores left and IKEA announced it is closing its 270,000 SF Cordova store.
Bookings start slow

Couples book their venue 12–18 months ahead, so a new hall needs about three years to fill: roughly 110–140 events in year 1 and 170–200 in year 2. Mid-market Memphis halls fill Saturdays only 3–9 months ahead and discount late dates (The Palace at Cordova sells dates inside 30 days from $3,500), and hotel ballrooms, the Esplanade and The Columns compete for large events.
Most weddings are smaller than these rooms

The average wedding has about 117 guests, and most Memphis halls hold 100–350. Two rooms have only 104 Saturdays a year between them, so most of the 215 events must be smaller events on other days. Without the movable walls that split each room, bookings could stay near 120–160 a year.
The building hides costs

A 1984 building converting to assembly use can need more fire alarm (voice evacuation above 1,000 occupants), exit, restroom and electrical work than estimated. The budget’s cushion for surprises covers some of this, not all.
Removing the columns costs more than assumed

The steel beams that replace the columns need sound footings at their ends and enough height below the roof. The budget is about $187,000 per column (about $0.7M for four), with the steel fabricator and structural engineer hired directly; contractor-delivered jobs elsewhere ran $207,000–480,000 per column.
One contractor does the whole job

The costs assume the ownership group manages the work and hires each trade directly. A general contractor typically adds about 11–22% for its overhead and profit: about $1.8M more for the efficient full plan, which would then take about 18.0 years instead of 16.3 to earn back, buying the property included.
The earthquake code applies
Memphis is near the New Madrid fault. If the large rooms together hold more than 2,500 people, the code can require strengthening the whole building, which could cost more than the columns.
The flood answer goes the wrong way

If the survey finds the floor below 250 ft, flood work rises toward the top of its range, about $0.85M instead of about $0.3M in the average case, and flood insurance costs more. The ground levels around the building make this unlikely.
The fuel pad stays empty
At average volumes a fuel company keeps only about $4 a year for every $100 it spends on a roughly $3.9M station, so a ground lease is not assured. The frontage parcel is also marketed on its own.
unknowns: Elevation certificate and boundary survey: finished floor against the 250 ft requirement, and the ground at the rear docks.
Structural engineer: roof framing, column and footing capacity, clear height, and a price for removing four columns.
Roof, rooftop units, electrical service, sprinkler riser and fire alarm: age and condition.
City letter confirming event halls, indoor recreation and fuel in CMU-3, and the zoning of the frontage parcel.
Phase I environmental assessment covering the former quick-lube on the frontage.
Commitments or letters of intent from caterers, a hall operator, a playground operator and shop tenants.

If the building’s large rooms (over 300 people each) add up to more than 2,500 people, the 2021 building code can require earthquake strengthening of the whole building. Capping each hall’s posted capacity is the likely fix; a structural engineer and the City must confirm.

purchase_assumption.note: Assumed price for planning. Fees, closing costs, surveys and inspections are added on top.

definitions.worst: A bad outcome: 1 in 10 simulated futures earn back more slowly.
definitions.realistic: The typical outcome: half of the simulated futures do better and half do worse.
definitions.best: A good outcome: 1 in 10 simulated futures earn back faster.

cases.method: Every input, from building costs and rents to hall bookings, prices and running costs, has a researched range: a bad end, a most likely value and a good end. 10,000 simulated futures let each input land anywhere in its range, more often near the most likely value, with related inputs moving together (bookings with prices, building costs with each other). Each case puts every input at the same point in its range, chosen so the efficient full plan matches the 1-in-10, typical and 1-in-10 results. Hall B is built in every case.

stress.note: Stress test, not a forecast: if every input sat at its bad end at the same time, the hall plans would lose money every year and never earn back; no more than 0.7% of the simulated futures did that badly. If every input sat at its good end at once, the plans would earn back in about 4–8 years; none of the simulated futures did that well.
